title: Not on the main plan
intro: Calvin wants to read these with the kids and decide later — nothing here is booked, and the pilgrimage week stays as written. Each card is a maybe: a short kid-friendly look, why it is optional instead of core, and a photo to talk around.

items.name: Domus Aurea (Nero’s Golden House)
items.callout: The kids learned about this in school
items.blurb: After the great fire of the year 64, Emperor Nero built a palace so huge people called it the Golden House — gold leaf, painted rooms, and a round hall that felt like dining under the stars. Later emperors buried most of it and built on top, so today you go downstairs into cool, dim rooms of frescoes. That hidden-palace feeling is why it stuck in the kids’ school lessons: it is a real place you can still walk through, not just a picture in a book.
items.whyOptional: It is not on the core itinerary, and it is not booked. Visits are usually guided and timed. There are stairs and underground stretches, which is a poor fit for a stroller, an 8-month-old, and all nine of you moving together. If you try it, it would be a small split group on a spare morning — talk it through first.
items.pairsWith: Near Friday’s Colosseum and Forum, but it is a separate timed visit — not an extra loop after lunch.
items.imageAlt: The octagonal hall of Nero’s Domus Aurea, with a round oculus in the concrete vault.
items.imageCredit: Photo: Mario Roberto Durán Ortiz (Mariordo) · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

items.name: Palatine Hill
items.blurb: Rome’s first houses stood on this hill. Emperors later built palaces among the umbrella pines. You walk brick ruins and look down on the Forum like a living map.
items.whyOptional: Friday already does the Colosseum and the Forum. The Forum notes say skip a deep Palatine walk unless older kids insist — so this is an extra loop on the same hill, not a new day.
items.pairsWith: Easy add-on to Friday’s Forum day, if legs still work after lunch.
items.imageAlt: Palatine Hill trees and brick ruins seen from the Circus Maximus.

items.name: Piazza del Campidoglio
items.blurb: Michelangelo designed this calm square on Capitoline Hill. A bronze emperor sits on a horse in the middle. Kids can enjoy the paving, the statues, and the view over the Forum without going inside.
items.whyOptional: The square itself is a short outdoor stop near Friday’s ruins. The Capitoline Museums are a separate indoor visit — optional, and easy to skip with a baby.
items.pairsWith: Close to Friday’s Forum / Piazza Venezia side. Museums optional; the piazza is the point.
items.imageAlt: Piazza del Campidoglio, the Michelangelo square on Capitoline Hill, with the statue of Marcus Aurelius.
items.imageCredit: Photo: Nhartmannphotos · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

items.name: Jewish Ghetto / Portico d’Ottavia
items.blurb: A neighborhood stroll past old Roman columns — the Portico of Octavia, once a grand gateway — and into the streets of Rome’s historic Jewish quarter. Short, outdoor, and full of stories.
items.whyOptional: Sunday lunch is already planned near here, by the Tiber. This is a walk before or after that meal, not a new destination across town.
items.pairsWith: Pairs with Sunday’s Tiber Island lunch area.
items.imageAlt: The brick and stone columns of the Portico of Octavia in Rome’s Jewish Ghetto.
items.imageCredit: Photo: Rabax63 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

items.name: Villa Borghese gardens
items.blurb: A big green park with ponds, paths, and room to run. After churches and stones, this is a kid reset: sit on the grass, watch the water, let the toddler burn energy.
items.whyOptional: Thursday stays close to Prati for the anniversary handoff. The gardens are a taxi or metro ride — better as a spare-day outing than squeezing into a pilgrimage day.
items.pairsWith: Light / spare-day kid reset (Monday pack day, or a quiet afternoon if energy is low).
items.imageAlt: The Piazza di Siena oval in Villa Borghese gardens, lined with pines and stone seating.
items.imageCredit: Photo: Diego Delso · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

items.name: Trajan’s Column / Markets
items.blurb: A tall marble comic-strip in stone: Trajan’s wars spiral up the column. Next door, the brick Markets of Trajan look like an ancient shopping mall from the street.
items.whyOptional: You can see the column and the market façades from outside, without another museum ticket. It sits between the Forum area and Piazza Venezia — a pause, not a third ruins site for Friday.
items.pairsWith: Street-side look near Friday’s Forum walk; skip going inside unless a split group really wants it.
items.imageAlt: Trajan’s Column standing beside the church of the Santissimo Nome di Maria in Trajan’s Forum.
items.imageCredit: Photo: Raffaele pagani · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

items.name: Baths of Caracalla
items.blurb: Giant open-air brick halls where Romans once swam and exercised. Kids can feel the scale — walls as tall as apartment buildings, with sky instead of a roof.
items.whyOptional: A separate site south of the Forum, so it needs its own outing. Ground is uneven; a stroller is awkward. Better as a spare-day walk than an add-on after Colosseum legs.
items.pairsWith: Spare day only. Open-air, but the stroller caveat is real.
items.imageAlt: Open-air brick ruins of the Baths of Caracalla under a blue sky.
items.imageCredit: Photo: Vyacheslav Argenberg · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

items.name: Ostia Antica
items.blurb: Rome’s old port town — a quieter kind of Pompeii. Streets, shops, a theatre, mosaics. Room to wander without city traffic.
items.whyOptional: This is a half-day train trip, not a nearby add-on. Monday’s spare day could take a half group (older kids + one adult) while others pack or stay in Prati.
items.pairsWith: Spare day / half group. Not a full-family-of-9 outing.
items.imageAlt: The brick theatre at Ostia Antica, Rome’s ancient port town.
items.imageCredit: Photo: Rabax63 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

items.name: Galleria Borghese
items.blurb: A villa-museum of Bernini statues and Caravaggio paintings. Quiet rooms, and marble that looks like real fabric — better for older kids and adults who already like art.
items.whyOptional: Timed tickets in small slots. Not a stroller museum, and not a full-family stop. A split group could peel off if you also walk the Villa Borghese gardens.
items.pairsWith: Same park as the gardens. Tickets are timed; nothing is reserved for this trip.
items.imageAlt: The garden façade of the Galleria Borghese villa.
items.imageCredit: Photo: Alessio Damato · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

items.name: St Peter’s Grottoes / Confessio
items.blurb: Downstairs from the basilica, a quieter crypt level near the traditional tomb of St Peter. Short, prayerful, and dim.
items.whyOptional: Wednesday already includes the basilica after the audience. The grottoes are a small extra if the group is calm — skip if anyone is done, and skip with a fussy baby.
items.pairsWith: Short add if everyone is still calm after the basilica on Vatican day.
items.imageAlt: The Confessio under the papal altar in St Peter’s, looking toward the niche of the pallia.
items.imageCredit: Photo: Dnalor 01 · CC BY-SA 3.0 AT · Wikimedia Commons

items.name: Vatican Museums + Sistine Chapel
items.blurb: Long museum halls ending at Michelangelo’s Sistine Chapel ceiling. Amazing — and also a lot of walking, queues, and “please be quiet” for little ones.
items.whyOptional: Already noted as an open item: optional for older kids plus one adult on a weekday, with a timed ticket. The rest of the group skips. Not on the core pilgrimage plan. Museums are typically closed Sunday.
items.pairsWith: The Wednesday afternoon note already allows this as an older-kids split. Still not booked.
items.imageAlt: The pine-cone courtyard of the Vatican Museums, with the bronze pigna under its niche.

items.name: St Peter’s dome climb
items.blurb: Stairs inside Michelangelo’s dome — close-up mosaics, then a view over the square. Tight passages, many steps, no stroller.
items.whyOptional: The arrival walk and Wednesday basilica visit both skip the dome with the baby and toddler. Only a split group of sure-footed older kids and adults.
items.pairsWith: Split group only, after the basilica, if energy and stairs allow.
items.imageAlt: Looking up into the mosaic-covered interior of St Peter’s dome.
items.imageCredit: Photo: Wknight94 · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

items.name: Scavi necropolis tour
items.blurb: An underground walk through the ancient cemetery beneath the basilica, near the area of St Peter’s tomb. Fascinating, tight, and serious.
items.whyOptional: Advance booking, age limits, and small-group rules. It is not a visit for nine people together, and it is a poor fit for a baby or toddler. Leave it off unless two adults can go another time.
items.pairsWith: Not for the full family of 9. Do not plan this as a group activity.
items.imageAlt: Brick tombs along a narrow street in the Vatican Necropolis beneath St Peter’s.
items.imageCredit: Photo: Blue 439 · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

items.name: Vatican Gardens
items.blurb: Quiet lawns and paths behind the Vatican walls — a green pause after stone and crowds.
items.whyOptional: Usually tour-only, with set times. Not a drop-in playground. If you try it, it would be a booked split-group tour, not a family wander. Nothing is reserved.
items.pairsWith: Tour-only extra; not a substitute for a park day (see Villa Borghese).
items.imageAlt: Formal hedges, lawn, and a fountain in the Vatican Gardens.
items.imageCredit: Photo: Staselnik · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

items.name: Vatican Post Office stamp stop
items.blurb: A tiny, fun stop: mail a postcard with a Vatican stamp from a kiosk in St Peter’s Square or the post office nearby. Kids love dropping a card in a different country’s mailbox.
items.whyOptional: Takes a few minutes before or after the basilica. No extra day and no tickets — just stamps and a postcard if the window is open.
items.pairsWith: Fun tiny add on Vatican day, if the kiosk is open and nobody is melting down.
items.imageAlt: The small Vatican post office kiosk on St Peter’s Square.
items.imageCredit: Photo: Ypsilon from Finland · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
